While a scene is open for editing (bank page, F3 Edit), the F keys show and change that scene's tracks; going back saves them and your live F keys come back.

docs.title: The scene bank
docs.text:
Press Performance again on the Performance screen to open the scene bank page: 16 scenes, with the ones on A and B marked.

Key Does Arrows, encoder or pads Select a scene. F1 Set A / F2 Set B Put the selected scene on the fader's A / B end. F3 Edit Open the scene on the Performance screen ("Editing scene N"): the pads set its rows, and you hear them as you go. Going back saves it. F4 Clear Clear the selected scene. F5 Export Save the columns and scenes as a bank file (see below). F6 Import Load a bank file into this project. F7 Ranges Set where on the fader each column moves (see below). F8 Back or Performance Back to playing. Play Start / stop, as when playing (here and on the Import and Ranges pages).

Scenes can also be put on the fader by a song: see Song mode.

docs.title: Fader ranges
docs.text:
By default every column moves across the whole fader: as you push from A to B, all of them change together. A fader range gives a column its own part of the fader, so one push can play a sequence of changes. For example, to build up:

Column Scene A Scene B Range LP cutoff -60 (closed) 0 (open) 0–33: opens first Delay send — +60 33–66: then the delay comes in Step Repeater — 1/16 at 66: then the rolls start

Scenes A and B stay the same; the range only sets when during the push each column goes from its A value to its B value. Before its range a column holds A's value, after it B's. Pulling the fader back undoes the changes in reverse. A song slot's ramp moves the same fader, so it plays the sequence too.

Open the Fader Ranges page with F7 on the bank page:

Each column has a row: its bar shows its range between A (left) and B (right), and the red line is where the fader is now. Left of the bar is the value the column plays at A (red), right of it the value at B (blue); --- means that scene doesn't set the column, so it has no effect there. Columns that neither scene on A / B drives are grey. A stepped column (Repeater, Direction, Tape stop …) can't move gradually, so it has one switch point instead (at 50 by default).

Key Does Up / Down or a pad Select a column. F1 Start / F2 End Toggle that edge on or off, like Rec. While one is on, its key is framed and the edge is in brackets ([0]-100). A stepped column's switch point moves with either. Encoder With Start or End on: move that edge. With neither: move the fader, to hear the result without leaving the page. F3 Reset The selected column back to the whole fader (0–100). F8 Back Back to the bank page. Performance goes back to playing.

Ranges belong to the columns of the project and are saved with it and in exported bank files.

docs.title: Scene bank files
docs.text:
A scene bank is a whole kit in one file, so it can move from song to song: the 12 columns (each one's effect type, its three row values and a MIDI CC column's target), the 16 scenes with their F keys, and which scenes are on A and B. Bank files are Performance/Scenes/<name>.txt on the card.

  • F5 Export opens the keyboard with a name (the bank imported last, else the project's name). Save (F8) writes the file, and asks before overwriting one.
  • F6 Import lists the bank files. Move with the encoder or Up / Down, then press Import (F8). Because importing replaces this project's columns and scenes, it asks first. Cancel (F7) or Left closes the list. The live pad rows start empty, and the fader blends the bank's scenes on A and B.

With Performance presets set to Global in Config (the default), the columns are shared by every project, so importing a bank changes them everywhere, just as editing a column does. The scenes always belong to the project.

docs.title: The bank file
docs.text:
Bank files are text, so they can be written or changed on a computer:

# OpenTracker scene bank
column 1 = LP cutoff: -60 0 60
column 2 = Tape stop: 1 3 5
column 3 = MIDI CC: - 64 127 @ midi 2 slot A
column 4 = Master FX: 30 60 90 @ fx ECHO 2
column 5 = ---
scene 1 = 1 0 2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
scene 2 fx on = 1 2 9
a = 1
b = 2
  • column N = type: row 1 row 2 row 3. The type is written as it appears in the type list (any case), and --- means an empty column. Values must be in the type's range; a value outside it reads as 0. A MIDI CC column holds CC values 0–127 (- = off) and its target, @ midi 1-16 slot A-F. A Master FX column holds the parameter's values (- = off) and its target, @ fx ID ROW: the effect's id (DIRT, LOFI, CHOR, BBDC, ECHO, TAPE) and the row of its settings page (1 = the one after the on row; Echo: 1 Time, 2 Feedback ... 7 Mix).
  • scene N = ... lists twelve rows, one per column, from 0 to 3, where 0 means the scene doesn't drive that column. Scenes that aren't listed are empty.
  • scene N fx on = ... lists the tracks whose F key the scene turns on (none turns them all off). Leave the line out and the scene doesn't change the F keys.
  • a and b give the scenes on A and B.
  • range N = start end gives column N's fader range (0–100). Leave it out for the whole fader; a stepped column's switch point is written as range N = 66 66.
  • # starts a comment. Unknown lines are ignored.

docs.title: Master FX
docs.text:
Two effect types act on the whole mix (after all tracks and synths, before the limiter), instead of on each track:

  • DJ filter: one value from −100 to +100. Below 0 a low-pass sweeping down, above 0 a high-pass sweeping up, 0 off. It's smoothed, so pads and the fader don't click, and it uses no CPU while off.
  • Tape stop: momentary. Hold its pad and the mix slows down to a stop over 1 or 2 steps, beats or bars (the row's value); release and it spins back up. It borrows free sample memory while it runs (shared with resampling), so it can refuse when memory is full.

Set them like any column: in edit mode, Up / Down open the type list; DJ filter and Tape stop are at the end.

docs.title: MIDI CC columns
docs.text:
A MIDI CC column plays a parameter of an external synth: one of a MIDI instrument's CC slots A–F, on that instrument's channel. Set it up in the type list: highlight MIDI CC, press Right to pick the MIDI instrument (shown with its preset name), Right again to pick the slot (shown with its CC name), then OK (F8).

  • The column is labelled with the instrument and the CC's name, e.g. MIDI 3 Cutoff. Which CC a slot sends is set on the MIDI instrument's parameters page, so change it there and the column follows.
  • Rows hold a value 0–127 (an empty row, ---, is off). A pad press sends its value; the fader, scenes and incoming CC send only when the value changes. Off, or leaving the screen, sends nothing, so the synth keeps its last value.
  • Several MIDI CC columns play at once, one per parameter. Two columns on the same slot are like two columns of one type: pressing one turns the other off.
  • Scenes fade each MIDI CC column on its own, so the fader (or a song's slot ramp) sweeps a synth's filter as it does a sample filter. A scene that doesn't drive the column leaves it at the other scene's value: a CC has no "off" value to fade to.
  • If the instrument's MIDI LFO is on the same slot, the column sets the LFO's Center, as a CC step FX does, and the LFO keeps swinging around it.

docs.title: Master FX columns
docs.text:
A Master FX column plays a setting of one of the master effects from the pads: for example Echo Feedback on three pads, or the Echo's Mix on the fader, for dub throws. Set it up in the type list: highlight Master FX (the last type), press Right to pick the effect, Right again to pick its setting, then OK (F8).

  • The column is labelled with the effect and the setting, e.g. Echo Feedback. Rows show values as the effect's page does (1/8 for an Echo time).
  • While a row of the column plays, the effect is on, with that setting changed. Tap the top (off) row and it goes back to how the FX bank has it: if it was off there, it turns off, and an Echo plays its repeats out. Leaving the screen does the same.
  • What the pads play is never saved into the effect: its page and the project keep your settings.
  • Several columns can play one effect, each a different setting (Echo Time on one, Feedback on another). Two columns on the same setting are like two columns of one type: pressing one turns the other off.
  • Scenes fade each Master FX column on its own. A scene that doesn't drive the column has the effect off there, so the effect comes in (or goes) at the middle of the fader, and its setting fades when both scenes drive it.
  • Effects on the card load when you choose them: moving to the settings list loads the effect so its settings show, and OK keeps it loaded while a column uses it, even when it's off in the FX bank. While the song plays, loading waits for Stop ("loads at Stop").

docs.title: Saved with the project
docs.text: The scene bank, the F keys (live and per scene), the master FX, MIDI CC and Master FX types, the MIDI CC columns' instruments and slots, the Master FX columns' effects and settings and the fader ranges are stored in perf_scenes.bin next to project.mt. Stock firmware and the Tracker Mini see those columns as empty and ignore the scenes.

docs.title: Remote control
docs.text: A Tracker running OpenTracker can be connected to a computer over USB and driven from it: as the simulator's front panel, by test scripts, or mirrored live on screen.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
1. Connect the Tracker by USB.
  2. Config > USB > Remote control: On. It's Off again after every power-on.
  3. On Linux the Tracker appears as a serial port, usually /dev/ttyACM0. If it can't be opened, add your user to the group that owns it (uucp on Arch, dialout on Debian/Ubuntu).

One program at a time

The link shares the USB serial port with the diag log. Close serial terminals, loggers or anything else that holds the port open first.

A short press of the power switch ends remote control (holding it still powers off).

docs.title: Drive mode: scripts
docs.text:
tools/tracker_remote.py presses buttons and pads, turns the encoder, reads the Tracker's status (screen, transport, output level, CPU, the current notice), the text on screen, and takes screenshots. The Tracker's own controls keep working.

tools/tracker_remote.py /dev/ttyACM0 -c "tap PERFORMANCE; wait 300; expect-screen Performance; text; screenshot perf.png" \
    --out shots --log tracker.log
  • Scripts use the simulator's script language plus checks (expect-text, expect-sound, wait-for slot == 2 …). Ready-made ones are in tools/remote_scripts/; the same files run on the simulator in CI.
  • open, play and stop call the Tracker directly instead of pressing keys, so a script doesn't depend on screen layouts: open Projects/Bench/OT Pool 1 - ACD opens that project and waits until it's loaded. It refuses while there are unsaved changes; open -f … drops them. The status shows the open project as proj=.
  • --log keeps everything the Tracker sends, including its telemetry lines. Check them with tools/telemetry_check.py log tracker.log.

Edit mode

In the Pattern screen's edit mode, the encoder and pads change the pattern. Turn edit mode off before running scripts that use them there.

docs.title: Live mirror
docs.text:
The simulator shows the Tracker's screen live and sends its window's keys and mouse to the Tracker:

build/full/sim/opentracker-sim --mirror /dev/ttyACM0

The Tracker sends each frame it draws (about 12 per second while playing).

docs.title: Panel mode
docs.text:
The Tracker becomes the simulator's front panel: its buttons, pads and encoder drive the simulator, and the simulator lights its pads.

build/full/sim/opentracker-sim --remote /dev/ttyACM0

The Tracker shows "Remote control: panel drives the simulator" and stops reacting to its own controls until the simulator quits or the cable is unplugged (it recovers within 2 s).

docs.title: Live resampling
docs.text: Record the master mix, one track (including the synth it plays) or Line in while the sequencer keeps playing, Octatrack-style. The take starts on the next bar and lasts 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 bars, or until you stop it. It lands in an instrument slot, ready to play, slice or re-record.

docs.title: Open the Resample screen
docs.text:
• While playing, press Sample Recorder. The Tracker asks "This will stop the pattern"; press Resample (F6) instead. The pattern keeps playing.
  • Shift + Sample Recorder arms, stops or cancels a take from any screen, with the Resample screen's current settings.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Column (key) Choices From (F1) Master (after the limiter; what the computer records over USB audio, without the USB input), Track 1–8, listed by their names (the track's sample voice plus the synth notes it plays, dry), Line in (with the recorder's channel mode), USB (what the computer plays into the Tracker, USB audio). Length (F2) Manual (until you stop it, snapped to a bar) or 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 bars. Slices (F3) Off, Per beat, Per step (equal slices), Beat hits, Step hits (a slice only where a new hit starts, so empty steps stay empty). Into (F4) New (the next free instrument) or instrument 1–48 (re-record into it). Place on (F5) Off or Track 1–8 (by name): write the take onto a track. A green track is free in the current pattern; a red one already has notes, which stay and cut the take off where they play. Gain, Monitor (F6, F7) Line in only: the recorder's input gain and monitoring. Record (F8) Arm: the take starts on the next bar (or with Play). Press again to stop at the next bar.

The right-hand column shows the take's state (Ready, Armed, Recording …) and, for Line in, a level meter.

docs.title: Where the take goes
docs.text:
• Into: New puts the take into the next free instrument above every loaded one, in stereo, so no playing sample moves. It's saved with the project.
  • Into: Instrument N re-records into N:
    • a take of the same length overwrites N in place, without a gap, and keeps N's settings, so a loop can be re-sampled take after take while it plays;
    • a take of another length isn't lost: it's saved as a new instrument, and a notice says so.
    • Arming into a slot that holds a sample asks once.
  • The take records into the free sample memory, which is reserved while it runs. The Sample Loader's memory bar counts it, and loading a sample during a take says why it can't.

docs.title: Slices and Place on
docs.text:
• With Slices on, the take becomes a Beat Slice instrument: note 24 + i (pad i + 1) plays slice i. At most 48 slices; the grid doubles until they fit.
  • Place on track N writes the take onto the track's first step, repeating every take length, or, when sliced, each slice on its own step, so the Performance FX (Repeater, Play mode, Direction, Start pos) work on it in time. Place on can be undone.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Resampling a track records it dry: no delay or reverb sends, no master FX.
  • The diag log on USB gets one line per take (frames, silent blocks, peak, input health), useful when a Line in take has dropouts.

docs.title: Song mode
docs.text:
The Song screen arranges patterns into a list of slots. The fork adds repeat counts, a Performance scene per slot, and fader ramps between two scenes, so a song can be arranged with performance changes without copying patterns, and progressions: chord patterns added in the order of a chord progression.

The track grid shows 8 tracks at a time: tracks 1-8 (the sample tracks), and tracks 9-16 (the MIDI tracks) once the grid cursor moves past track 8. The space this frees shows each pattern's name next to its number, as on stock.

The Song list has four columns: Pattern, Count, Scene and Ramp. In edit mode (Rec), Right moves from the list into the columns, Left back. Delete resets the selected value.

docs.title: Repeat counts
docs.text:
• Count plays the slot's pattern 1 to 16 times before the song moves on, so a section no longer needs duplicate slots. Set it with the encoder.
  • While playing, the playing slot shows its pass, for example 3/4.
  • Add Slot copies the count. Loop Pattern / Continue Song work as before (Continue leaves the slot at the end of the current pass).

docs.title: Scenes per slot
docs.text:
• Scene puts a scene from the scene bank on the crossfader's A end as the slot starts, with the fader at A. The encoder picks the scene, or - for none.
  • Shift + encoder adds a second scene for B (shown as 3>4).
  • A slot's scene plays on any screen, not only on the Performance screen, until Stop or the next slot.
  • A - slot (no scene): on the Performance screen what plays stays; on other screens the song's scene ends (FX off). To hold a scene across slots, set it on each slot.

docs.title: Ramps
docs.text:
A ramp is the song moving the crossfader for you. For example, a build-up into a drop: scene 1 is the mix dry and open, scene 2 has the low-pass filter nearly closed and lots of delay. A slot plays pattern 5 with Count 4, Scene 1>2 and Ramp Slot: over its four passes the filter closes slowly, by itself, on any screen. The next slot starts with its own scene, so the drop comes in clean.

A slot with a scene on B sweeps the fader from A to B, and Ramp sets when. On that 4-pass slot, the fader moves like this:

pass:  1         2         3         4
Slot   A ──────────────────────────────────→ B  one slow sweep over all 4
Each   A ────→ B A ────→ B A ────→ B A ────→ B  a sweep each pass, back to A
First  A ────→ B B ······· B ······· B ·······  sweeps on pass 1, then stays on B
Last   A ······· A ······· A ······· A ────→ B  only the last pass
L2     A ······· A ······· A ──────────────→ B  the last 2 passes
16     A ······· A ······· A ······· A ···─→ B  only the last 16 steps (a fill)
Ramp The fader goes A → B … Slot across all the slot's passes Each across each pass, back to A as the next one starts First across the first pass, then stays on B Last, L2 … L15 across the last N passes (the choices follow the slot's Count) 1 … 128 across the slot's last N steps (Shift + encoder moves by 16)

A slot with only an A scene (3) has no ramp: it plays scene 3 the whole slot. Moving the fader yourself takes over until the next slot.

docs.title: Moving around
docs.text: • Song + Right jumps from the track grid straight to the Pattern list; Song + Left goes back into the grid (edit mode). Shift + Left / Right still sizes the grid selection.

docs.title: Progressions
docs.text:
A common way to write chords on the Tracker is one chord per pattern, each pattern named after its chord, with Song mode putting them in order. Insert (in edit mode) does that for you: pick a progression and it adds the slots, with a named pattern for each chord.

For example, in A minor (Config > Project Settings: Root note A, Scale Minor), press Rec, then Insert, pick Am F C G i VI III VII and press F8 Insert. Four slots appear after the cursor, playing four patterns named Am i, F VI, C III and G VII, each with its chord on step 1 of tracks 1-3, using the current instrument. The cursor ends on the last of them, so a second Insert (a chorus, say) follows on. Press F2 Play Song to hear it, then open each pattern to give the chord a rhythm, add drums, or change the voicing.

  • The Pattern list shows each pattern's name, so the song reads as its chords.
  • The list shows each progression's chords in the project key, with its numbers (or its title) on the right, under a heading per file. Up / Down or the encoder pick one, F8 or Insert adds it as a slot per chord, F5 as one pattern (below), F7 or Left closes the list.
  • A chord that already has a pattern named after it reuses that pattern (only the name's first word is checked, so a pattern you called F counts as F). A chord that comes twice in a progression gets one pattern.
  • New chords go into empty, unnamed patterns that aren't in the song yet. Nothing you made is overwritten. If the cursor slot holds an empty, unnamed pattern (a new project's slot 1), the progression starts there instead of after it.
  • New patterns take the track lengths of the cursor slot's pattern. Sevenths use tracks 1-4.
  • The numbers are worked out from the key when you add the progression. Changing the key later leaves the pattern names as they are.

docs.title: Voicing
docs.text:
The same chord can be stacked in different shapes: Am is A, C and E, close together or spread out. F6 Voicing in the list picks the shape before you press F8. Each press shows the first two chords' notes, for example Smooth: Am A4 C5 E5 > F A4 C5 F5.

Voicing What it writes Good for Smooth each chord in the shape closest to the one before, so the notes move little (A and C stay from Am to F) pads and keys; the default Block every chord in root position, root in the C4 octave stabs, a plain chord sound Wide the root an octave lower, then the 5th, the 3rd an octave up big pads, strings Bass the root an octave lower on its own track, the chord above it (Smooth) giving the bass its own instrument afterwards; uses one more track

  • A voicing other than Smooth adds its name to each pattern's name (Am i Wide), and a chord is only reused from a pattern with the same voicing. So you can insert a verse Smooth and a chorus Wide, and the chorus gets its own patterns:

  • The choice stays until the Tracker is switched off.
  • A reused pattern keeps its notes: a chord that comes twice is one pattern, voiced the first time. To change a single chord's shape, open its pattern and move the notes.

docs.title: One pattern to resample
docs.text:
F5 Insert Pattern adds the progression as a single pattern instead: one slot playing a pattern named after its chords (Am F C G), with a chord on the first step of each bar (16 steps in 4/4), so four chords make a 64-step pattern and eight fill 128. Voicing works the same (Am F C G Wide), and the same progression in the same voicing reuses its pattern.

That pattern is made to be resampled and chopped, the way a sampled record is flipped:

  1. Play it with the sound you want, then resample it from Master for as many bars as it has chords (see Resampling), with Slices: Step hits. The slices go where a new sound starts, so a sound with a slow fade-in may not mark every chord change; take it with a sharper sound (or a shorter attack) instead.
  2. The take is a Beat Slice instrument with a slice per chord: pad 1 plays the first chord, pad 2 the second, each at its own pitch.
  3. Put the slices in a new order, cut them short, or play them with the Performance FX.

To play one chord at other pitches instead (a chord stab), set the instrument to Slice, pick the chord with the Slice FX and play it from the pads.

docs.title: The progression files
docs.text:
The list comes from text files in Progressions/ on the card, one heading per file (Jazz.txt shows as Jazz). The first time you open the list with no files there, the Tracker writes its own: DnB, Hip-hop, Jazz and Pop. Edit them, add your own, or copy them to share; a file of yours is never overwritten. To get the built-in files back, delete or rename them.

Each line is one progression, written as numbers so the same file works in any key:

# Jazz.txt
ii7 V7 Imaj7 | Two-five-one
iim7b5 V7 i
i VI III VII | Jungle pads
  • I to VII are the chords on the 1st to 7th note of the key. Upper case is a major chord, lower case a minor one.
  • After the number: 7 (a 7th: dominant on upper case, minor on lower), maj7, m7, dim, dim7, m7b5, aug, sus2, sus4.
  • b or # in front lowers or raises the chord's root a semitone (bVII in C is Bb).
  • Chords are built as written, even when that takes a note from outside the key: V in a minor key is a major chord (E in A minor), as it usually is in minor.
  • Major or minor: start a line with major: or minor: to say which key it is in (minor: iv V). Without it, the Tracker picks the key whose own chords the line uses most: iv V and iv VII III VI are minor (Dm E and Dm G C F in A minor), I V vi IV is major. In a minor key the numbers count on the natural minor scale (VI in A minor is F), and viidim / viidim7 sit on the raised 7th, as in harmonic minor (G#dim in A minor).
  • In the project key: a scale with a minor 3rd and no major 3rd counts as minor (Minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Locrian, Harm Min, ...), any other as major (Major, Lydian, Mixolydian, Chromatic, ...). A progression of the same kind plays on the project's root note; one of the other kind plays in the relative key. In A minor, I V vi IV gives C G Am F.
  • Modes play progressions as their parallel major or minor key. D Dorian counts as D minor: i IV gives Dm G and I V vi IV gives F C Dm Bb. Chords that use the note where the mode differs from plain minor or major leave the mode's scale (the Bb above; Dorian has B).
  • Names: with Note names on Auto (Config > General) chords are spelled from the key: each number has its own letter, so bVII in C is Bb and vii dim in F# major is E#dim, not Fdim. With Sharps or Flats, every chord name follows that setting (bVII in C shows as A# with Sharps); the notes always sound the same.
  • The numbers in a pattern's name are the progression's, as written: in A minor, I V vi IV names its first pattern C I.
  • Text after | is the title shown in the list. Lines starting with # are comments. Lines that can't be read are skipped; the list says how many.

docs.title: Saved with the project
docs.text: Counts, scenes and ramps are stored in song.bin next to project.mt. Stock firmware plays every slot once, without scenes.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
File > Export > Song and Song Stems render the slots' scenes and ramps the way playback does. F7 Perf FX on the Export page turns this On / Off (On after every power-on); Off gives the stock export without Performance FX.

  • Stems get each track's Performance FX. The master FX (DJ filter, tape stop) act on the whole mix, so only the full-mix export (Song) has them.
  • Only what the song stores is rendered: where the fader or the pads were when you pressed Export doesn't matter, so the same song always exports the same way.
  • Pattern exports play no song slots, so they render without scenes.

docs.title: Track timing
docs.text: Give each track of a pattern its own speed and groove. For example: hats at 2x over a kick at 1x, a bass at 1/2x that takes two loops of the pattern to play its 16 steps, drums on Swing 58 while the keys stay Straight.

docs.title: Setting it
docs.text:
On the Pattern screen, press More (F8) twice for the names page:

Key Does Speed (F3) Hold and turn the encoder (or Up / Down): 1/8x, 1/4x, 1/2x, 3/4x, 1x, 1.5x, 2x. Groove (F4) Hold and turn: Global, Straight, Swing 54, 58, 62, 66, 71, Shuffle, Laid back.
  • They set the cursor track of the current pattern. While holding F3 or F4, Left / Right moves to the next track, so you can set several in one go.
  • A track off the defaults shows a tag in its header: Hats 2x, Kick 3/4x S58, Keys Str. A pattern with every track at 1x / Global looks as on stock.
  • Undo takes a change back. Copying a pattern copies its timing.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
• Speed changes when steps play, never how they sound: a sample keeps its pitch and length, so at 2x a long sample is cut by the next note on the track.
  • Things counted in steps follow the track: Roll, Arp, Micro-move, Gate and the groove. Things counted in time don't: envelopes, LFOs, Timestretch.
  • The pattern still ends after its length at 1x, and song mode moves on then. A track at another speed wraps on its own length: at 2x it loops twice per pattern, at 1/2x it plays half its steps per pattern and carries on from there the next time round. Switching to another pattern starts every track from step 1 again.
  • MIDI clock out, the metronome and the playhead row follow the pattern at 1x.

docs.title: Groove
docs.text:
• Global (default): the track swings with the Swing step FX, as on stock.
  • Any other groove replaces the Swing FX for that track: Straight keeps it even while the rest swings; Swing 54–71 delays every second step by that much (MPC style: 54 is a light lilt, 66 close to triplets); Shuffle swings 8th notes; Laid back plays beats 2 and 4 a little late.
  • A groove moves notes by where they sit in the bar, so notes you add later get it too. Micro-move still nudges a single note on top.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: The settings are saved in timing.bin next to project.mt, only while a pattern uses them. Stock firmware and the Tracker Mini ignore the file and play every track at 1x with the Swing FX.

docs.title: The Tracker doesn't start, or keeps restarting
docs.text:
• Go back to stock: put the stock image's file name (for example PolyendTracker_1.9.2.ptf) in /Firmware/ot_restore.txt on the card and power-cycle. This runs before the rest of OpenTracker. See Install and go back.
  • The update bootloader and the rear reset button are never touched by OpenTracker; the worst case is reflashing.

docs.title: "Restarted after a crash (stack overflow)"
docs.text:
OpenTracker has a stack guard: a protected memory area below the stack. If the stack ever overflows into it, the Tracker resets cleanly instead of silently corrupting memory, and after the restart it shows "Restarted after a crash (stack overflow)" for a few seconds. The diag log records "reset reason: core lockup".

  • Please report it as an issue, with what you were doing and, if possible, the diag log.
  • To run without the guard (for example to compare), create an empty file /Firmware/ot_noguard.txt.

docs.title: Sound problems
docs.text:
• Crackles or dropped notes when busy: check the CPU meter (Config > General > CPU meter). The voice limiter cuts synth voices first when the audio gets close to its limit; lowering Synth voices or synth polyphony helps.
  • A synth slot is silent and shows "not available": its model is a card module that isn't on the card, or is from another firmware version. Copy the release's Modules folder to the card (Install the modules).
  • DX7 voice sounds different from a hardware DX7: report the voice (.syx file) in an issue; the engine is checked against Dexed, not hardware.

docs.title: The diag log and telemetry
docs.text:
Over USB, the Tracker also appears as a serial port with a diag log: boot messages, warnings, and every 5 seconds a telemetry line:

telemetry: render cyc/block min … avg … max … | loop max … ms | stack peak … B heap … B of … B (free … B) | rx restarts … stale …
  • render: audio CPU per 128-sample block (the budget is 522,240 cycles).
  • loop max: the slowest main-loop pass (UI, SD card).
  • stack peak / free: the deepest stack use since boot and what's left.
  • rx restarts / stale: Line in health (I2S input restarts and stale blocks).

Read it with any serial terminal, or capture it with tools/tracker_remote.py --log. tools/telemetry_check.py log FILE checks a captured log against the thresholds.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: See Home.

docs.title: USB audio
docs.text:
The Tracker shows up on a computer as a USB sound card, OpenTracker, next to its USB MIDI, serial and storage. Whatever the computer plays into it (a browser, a DAW, a software synth) can be heard through the Tracker and sampled with it, and the computer can record the Tracker. No driver needed.

Works with Linux and Windows. macOS sees the device but isn't supported: it can't follow the Tracker's clock, so expect a click every half-minute or so.

docs.title: Hear the computer
docs.text:
1. Connect the Tracker over USB and pick OpenTracker as the computer's audio output.
  2. On the Tracker, open the Global Mixer (Master, three presses) and unmute USB (F8), the last column.

Like Line in, USB starts muted in a new project. Its column works like the others: hold F8 and turn the encoder for the level, hold F8 + Delete for 0 dB, Shift + F8 to solo it. The level and mute are saved with the project.

USB audio joins the mix after the limiter, under master volume: the delay and reverb sends don't get it, and it isn't sent back to the computer (see below).

docs.title: Sample the computer
docs.text:
• Sample Recorder: Source USB (the fifth, after Mic HG). Always stereo, no Gain. With Monitor On you hear it at full level whatever the mixer says, as with Line in.
  • Resample: From USB records it on the bar, like Line in. You hear it through the Global Mixer USB column.

docs.title: Record the Tracker on the computer
docs.text:
Pick OpenTracker as the input in the DAW or recorder and record. The computer gets the Tracker's master bus, the same signal Resample From Master takes:

  • After the limiter and before master volume: turn the Tracker down for listening without changing the recording level.
  • Line in is in it when unmuted in the Global Mixer, so the Tracker also works as the sound card for whatever is plugged into it.
  • File preview is in it (Sample Loader Preview, the Preview buttons), so you can audition samples when you listen over USB.
  • Not in it: the metronome and the computer's own USB audio. A DAW that records the Tracker while playing through it doesn't record its own playback again.

Nothing to turn on: it's sent while the computer records.

To just listen on Linux, tools/usb_listen.sh links the Tracker to the computer's output (tools/usb_listen.sh off removes it; run it again after the Tracker reconnects). Easy Effects moves every recording stream, a DAW's included, onto its own microphone input: the Tracker then sounds silent. Turn off its Process all inputs, or exclude the app.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Latency is about 5 ms each way on the Tracker plus the computer's own buffer: fine for sampling, recording and listening along, not for playing a software synth live from the pads.
  • The Tracker runs at 44,117 Hz, a little over the 44,100 Hz it names. Linux and Windows adjust for that on their side when recording, as with any USB sound card.
  • The computer's volume control works as usual (the Tracker has no volume of its own on the USB side).
  • While USB Storage mode copies files, USB audio drops out.

docs.title: Synths
docs.text:
Every synth model, how it works and what each setting does. The Settings part of each page is also what the help box in Edit Patch shows.

Synth 8-Type A chip-style synth in the spirit of the 3-voice sound chips of 8-bit home computers: three oscillators with combined waves, ring modulation and sync, one multimode filter, a stepped envelope and the chip tricks. A-Type A two-oscillator synth that can play two notes at once, after the semi-modular duophonic synths of the 1970s: sync, ring modulation, sample & hold and two envelopes. ACD A one-oscillator acid synth after the Tracker Mini's ACD: saw, square, sub and noise into a resonant low-pass, with a modulation envelope, one LFO and glide. Arc-Type A chip-style FM voice in the spirit of the 4-operator FM sound chips of home consoles, with their square and noise companion: four sine operators, envelopes counted in chip rates, a 9-bit output and the chip arpeggio. B-Type A buzzy 8-bit chip voice: square waves, noisy buzz shapes, stepped volume and the fast arpeggios of old home computer music. CS-Type A polysynth with two layers per note, after the large dual-channel polysynths of the late 1970s: two full synth voices stacked, a ring modulator, and touch control. D-Type A three-oscillator synth with a ladder filter, after the classic monophonic synths of the early 1970s. DX7 A six-operator FM engine that plays Yamaha DX7 voices (.syx files). Loading voices, banks and playing are on the DX7 page. FAT A unison saw synth after the Tracker Mini's FAT: a stack of up to seven detuned saws into a low-pass filter, with one LFO and glide. FM4 A four-operator FM synth in the spirit of the classic 4-op FM chips: four sine operators in eight algorithms, feedback on operator 1, and an envelope per operator. Hand-Type A chip-style synth in the spirit of the 4-channel sound chip of a handheld console: one patch is one channel (Pulse, Wave or Noise) or a whole drum kit, with a stepped envelope and the chip tricks. JU6 A polysynth with one oscillator per voice, a resonant filter, one envelope and a built-in stereo chorus, after the one-oscillator polysynths of the early 1980s. PERC A drum machine after the Tracker Mini's PERC: one patch is a kit of six drums, each with its own mixer channel, and a waveshaper and EQ on the kit. T-Type A drum synth after the classic transistor drum machines: one patch is a kit of ten drum channels, every drum built from sines with pitch sweeps, filtered noise, struck resonators and a bank of six square oscillators. VAP A two-oscillator virtual analog polysynth after the Tracker Mini's VAP: oscillators that morph from triangle to saw to pulse, a 15-type filter, three envelopes, two LFOs and a modulation matrix. WTFM A two-operator FM synth with shapeable operators, after the Tracker Mini's WTFM: each operator plays a waveform row you can morph, operator 2 modulates operator 1, and a filter, three envelopes, two LFOs and a modulation matrix follow.

docs.title: 8-Type
docs.text:
A chip-style synth in the spirit of the 3-voice sound chips of 8-bit home computers: three oscillators with combined waves, ring modulation and sync, one multimode filter, a stepped envelope and the chip tricks.

8-Type is our own design from general knowledge of such chips, not a copy of any chip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each note plays three oscillators. Each one has a Wave: triangle, saw, pulse, noise, or a combined wave where the pulse switches the other wave on and off (Tri+Pulse, Saw+Pulse), or Tri+Saw, half of each. Off silences it. PW sets the pulse width and PWM Depth how far the slot's PWM LFO (PWM Rate in Voice) sweeps it.

Each oscillator links to the one before it: oscillator 2 to 1, 3 to 2, and 1 to 3. Sync restarts it each time that one starts a cycle. Ring flips its wave each time that one's square flips, and works on the waves with a triangle in them (Tri, Tri+Pulse, Tri+Saw).

Filt sends an oscillator through the filter or around it. The filter is a 12 dB multimode: Mode picks low-pass, band-pass, high-pass or a mix of them. Its Resonance has 16 steps and never sings on its own. Dirt drives it harder. A simple filter envelope jumps up at each note and falls back over Env Decay; Env Amt sets how far, up or down.

Grit steps the oscillators' mix to fewer bits, like a small converter; an oscillator with Clean On skips it. The volume Envelope is an ADSR with 16 steps per stage, timed from a table. The Chip Tricks add the chip arpeggio, a stepped vibrato and a slide into each note.

The Init patch plays oscillator 1 alone, a square through the low-pass filter. Oscillators 2 and 3 are Off.

docs.title: ACD
docs.text:
A one-oscillator acid synth after the Tracker Mini's ACD: saw, square, sub and noise into a resonant low-pass, with a modulation envelope, one LFO and glide.

ACD's sound engine is our own design, built to the Tracker Mini's ACD settings.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The oscillator mixes a saw, a square (a pulse whose width is PW), a sub oscillator one or two octaves down (Sub Mode) and noise. Plus Noise Mix puts the noise before the filter, minus after it.

The filter is a resonant low-pass: a 12 or 24 dB state-variable filter, or RD3, a 4-pole ladder with soft clipping in its feedback. Its cutoff moves with the Mod Env (Env Amt), the LFO (LFO Amt) and the note (Note Track).

The Amp Env shapes the volume. The Mod Env moves the cutoff and the pulse width (PW Env). The LFO can move the cutoff, the pulse width (PW LFO) and the pitch (Pitch LFO).

docs.title: Arc-Type
docs.text:
A chip-style FM voice in the spirit of the 4-operator FM sound chips of home consoles, with their square and noise companion: four sine operators, envelopes counted in chip rates, a 9-bit output and the chip arpeggio.

Arc-Type is our own design from general knowledge of such chips, not a copy of any chip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The four operators work as in FM4: each is a sine with a pitch multiple (MUL), a small detune (DT) and a Level. The Algorithm says which operators modulate which; the last operator in each chain is heard. Operator 1 can modulate itself (Feedback).

Each operator's envelope is set in chip rates, where a higher number is faster: AR (attack, 1 to 31; 0 never starts, so the operator stays silent), D1R (first decay) down to D1L (the first decay level, 3 dB a step), D2R (second decay while the note is held; 0 holds) and RR (release, 0 to 15). RS (rate scaling) makes all of an operator's rates faster on higher notes.

Loop makes an envelope repeat when it has fallen 48 dB: start the attack again, rise back up as a mirror image, or turn upside down.

One LFO (a triangle, shared by the slot's voices) moves the pitch (PMS) and, on each operator with AMS above 0, the level.

The DAC sets the output: Off is clean, 9-bit steps the wave to 9 bits, and Ladder adds uneven steps and a small gap around zero.

The Aux Voice adds a square or noise voice to each note, with a stepped decay. Chip Tricks are the chip arpeggio and a slide into each note, as on B-Type.

The Init patch is algorithm 1>2>3>4 with operator 3 at 25 % into operator 4, the only one heard. Operators 1 and 2 are at Level 0.

  • (1+2)>3>4: 1 and 2 both into 3, then into 4; only 4 is heard.
  • (1+2>3)>4: 1 into 4 and 2 into 3 into 4; only 4 is heard.
  • (1>2+3)>4: 1 into 2 into 4, and 3 into 4; only 4 is heard.
  • 1>2, 3>4: two pairs: 1 into 2 and 3 into 4; 2 and 4 are heard.
  • 1>(2,3,4): 1 into each of 2, 3 and 4; all three are heard.
  • 1>2, 3, 4: 1 into 2; 2, 3 and 4 are heard.
  • 1, 2, 3, 4: no modulation: four sines mixed.

docs.title: A-Type
docs.text:
A two-oscillator synth that can play two notes at once, after the semi-modular duophonic synths of the 1970s: sync, ring modulation, sample & hold and two envelopes.

A-Type is our own design from those instruments' owner's manuals, not a copy of any one of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Two VCOs each play a saw or a pulse. Each has a Range in octaves (32' is the lowest, 4' the highest) and a fine tune; VCO 2 can also be tuned in semitones. Sync restarts VCO 2 every time VCO 1 starts a new cycle. The two VCOs drift a little in pitch, as analog oscillators do.

The Mixer sets each VCO's level and adds a third source: noise, or the ring modulator (VCO 1 times VCO 2).

The Sample & Hold picks up a value from its input (noise, a VCO or the mix) at a steady Rate or on each new note (Clock Key), and holds it until the next one. Lag smooths the steps. S&H can move the filter cutoff (S&H Amt) and VCO 2's pitch (Mod Src S&H).

The Filter is a high-pass (HPF) and then a resonant low-pass: 4-pole (24 dB) or 2-pole (12 dB). Its cutoff moves with the note (Key Track), an envelope, the LFO and the S&H.

There are two envelopes: an ADSR and a simpler AR (attack, release). Each of the filter (Env Src) and the volume (VCA Env) uses one of them. One LFO is shared by the slot's voices.

Keyboard Duo (at Poly 1): when you hold two or more notes, VCO 1 plays the lowest and VCO 2 the highest; one note plays both. Priority picks which note wins at Poly 1.

docs.title: B-Type
docs.text:
A buzzy 8-bit chip voice: square waves, noisy buzz shapes, stepped volume and the fast arpeggios of old home computer music.

B-Type is modelled on the sound chips of 8-bit home computers and consoles, the kind with four simple channels and a handful of tricks. It is our own design from general knowledge of such chips, not a copy of any one of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each note is a square wave whose pitch comes from dividing a fixed chip clock. Real chips can only divide by whole numbers, so they can't hit every pitch exactly: Tuning chooses between exact pitches (Free) and the chip's own, slightly sour ones (Coarse, Fine).

Instead of a clean square, the chip can play the bits of its polynomial counters: short repeating bit patterns that turn the tone into a buzz, or with long patterns into noise. That's Distortion: Pure is the clean square, Poly4 to Poly17 are patterns from short (reedy) to long (noise), and the Poly5x combinations mix two of them. The Clock changes how fast the patterns run, so it changes the buzz too.

A second channel can play along a few divider steps away (Channel 2: Level, Detune), for a thicker, beating sound. The chip's high-pass trick (Hi-Pass, HP Freq) subtracts a delayed copy of the sound from itself, which thins and hollows it.

Volume moves in 16 steps at the chip's 60 frames a second (Envelope, with Bits On), and the output goes through a small DAC (DAC Bits: 4 for the real crunch, 8 for clean). On top sit the chip tricks: the fast arpeggio, vibrato and pitch slides that chip musicians used to fake chords and expression.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Tuning Coarse sounds like the real chip: high notes go out of tune. Free is better when B-Type plays with other instruments.
  • DAC Bits and Bits (the stepped envelope) are most of the "8-bit" character. Set both clean for a softer sound that keeps the buzz.
  • The help box on Edit Patch shows the reference below for whatever you're on.

docs.title: Distortion
docs.text:

  • Poly9: a longer pattern: rough and noisy.
  • Poly17: a very long pattern: close to noise, good for hats and snares.

  • Poly5x17: Poly5 with Poly17: grainy noise that still has a pitch.

docs.title: Arp Mode
docs.text:

  • Dom7: major with a flat 7th: bluesy.
  • Maj7: major with the 7th: soft and jazzy.
  • Min7: minor with the 7th: smooth and jazzy.
  • Dim: diminished: tense.
  • Aug: augmented: dreamy and unsettled.
  • Pow5: root and 5th: a power chord.

  • 1/48: 32nd-note triplets, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/64: a step every 64th note, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/96: 64th-note triplets, locked to the tempo.

docs.title: CS-Type
docs.text:
A polysynth with two layers per note, after the large dual-channel polysynths of the late 1970s: two full synth voices stacked, a ring modulator, and touch control.

CS-Type is our own design from those instruments' owner's manuals, not a copy of any one of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every note plays two layers, I and II. Each layer is a complete voice:

  • an oscillator with a saw and a pulse that can sound together (the pulse has its own PWM LFO), plus a sine and noise;
  • a resonant high-pass and a resonant low-pass filter (12 dB each);
  • a filter envelope, IL / AL: the cutoff starts at the Initial level, moves to the Attack level over F Attack, comes back to Initial over F Decay and stays there while the note is held, then returns to the LPF setting over F Release;
  • an amplifier with its own ADSR and level.

Layer II can be detuned against layer I (II Detune). Brilliance and Resonance move both layers' filters at once.

The two layers' sum goes through a ring modulator: a sine at RM Speed. RM Sweep starts it higher or lower and slides it to RM Speed over RM Decay.

A sub-oscillator LFO (Function, Speed) can move the pitch, the filters and the volume. Touch brings in the instrument's touch control: how hard you play the note (Init) changes the filter sweep and the level; the Touch setting stands in for pressing harder after the note started (After), and works best on a macro. The Ribbon bends the pitch; it's meant for a macro too.

docs.title: D-Type
docs.text:
A three-oscillator synth with a ladder filter, after the classic monophonic synths of the early 1970s.

D-Type is our own design from those instruments' owner's manuals, not a copy of any one of them. It's built as a mono synth: at Poly 1 it plays the last note held, with legato and glide.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Three VCOs play one of six waves each. Their Range is in octaves (32' is low, 2' is high) plus Lo, far below hearing, for using a VCO as a slow modulator. VCO 2 and VCO 3 can be tuned against VCO 1. VCO 3 can leave the keyboard (Keyboard Off): it then stays at one pitch whatever you play, which suits it as an LFO. The VCOs drift a little in pitch, as analog oscillators do.

The Mixer adds noise (white or pink) and Feedback, which sends the filter's output back into its input.

The Filter is a 4-pole ladder low-pass. Emphasis is its resonance: from about 75 % it sings on its own. The Filter Contour sweeps its cutoff up (Contour sets how far), and Key Track makes it follow the note.

The two contours are ADS envelopes: one for the filter, one for the volume (Loudness). There's no Release setting: Decay Sw On makes the release as long as Decay, Off makes it short.

Modulation: Mod Mix blends VCO 3 and the noise into one source. Osc Mod sends it to the pitch of VCO 1 and VCO 2, Filter Mod to the cutoff. Wheel sets how much of both gets through, like the modulation wheel; it's 0 in Init, so turn it up first.

docs.title: DX7
docs.text: A six-operator FM engine that plays Yamaha DX7 voices (.syx files). Loading voices, banks and playing are on the DX7 page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The sound is the loaded DX7 voice: its six operators, algorithm, envelopes and LFO, as programmed on a DX7. There's no operator editor. The settings here work on top of the voice without changing its data: Delete puts a setting back to 0 (or 100 %), and the voice sounds as it did on the DX7.

The Init patch puts M1–M6 on the six Tone settings, so a voice can be shaped from the Synth Macros page or with the macro FX without opening Edit Patch.

How much a Tone setting changes depends on the voice. Brightness does nothing on a voice whose operators are all carriers, and Feedback is only heard when the feedback operator is.

docs.title: FAT
docs.text:
A unison saw synth after the Tracker Mini's FAT: a stack of up to seven detuned saws into a low-pass filter, with one LFO and glide.

FAT's sound engine is our own design, built to the Tracker Mini's FAT settings.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each note plays a stack of saws: one in the middle and up to three detuned pairs. Fatness brings the pairs in (the first from just above 0, all three from about 67) and spreads them further apart. Timbre turns every saw towards a square, and Brightness closes a gentle low-pass on the stack. Stereo spreads the pairs left and right.

The filter is a 24 or 12 dB low-pass in two flavours, with the Filter Env and the LFO on its cutoff. The LFO can also move the stack's pitch (LFO Amt in Oscillator).

docs.title: FM4
docs.text:
A four-operator FM synth in the spirit of the classic 4-op FM chips: four sine operators in eight algorithms, feedback on operator 1, and an envelope per operator.

FM4 is our own design, not a copy of any instrument.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
FM4 has four operators, each a sine wave with its own pitch ratio (Mult), small Detune, Level and envelope. The Algorithm says how they connect: an operator that feeds another one is a modulator and changes its tone. An operator at the end of a chain is a carrier and is what you hear. In 1>2>3>4, operator 1 modulates 2, 2 modulates 3, 3 modulates 4, and only 4 is heard. In 1 + 2 + 3 + 4, all four are heard and none modulates.

A carrier's Level sets how loud it is. A modulator's Level sets how much it changes its target: the higher, the more overtones. Its envelope shapes that over the note, so a modulator that decays faster than its carrier makes the tone fade from bright to plain.

Operator 1 can also modulate itself (Feedback), which adds overtones to its sine.

Each operator's envelope has five stages: Attack up to full, Decay down to Sustain, then Sus Rate keeps fading while the note is held (0 holds it), and Release after the note ends. A voice ends when all its carriers are silent.

One LFO (a triangle) is shared by the slot's voices. Vibrato sends it to the pitch; Tremolo sends it to the level of each operator whose own Tremolo is On.

The Init patch is algorithm 1>2>3>4 with only operator 3 modulating the carrier, 4, a little. Operators 1 and 2 are at Level 0, so turn them up to hear what they add.

docs.title: Hand-Type
docs.text:
A chip-style synth in the spirit of the 4-channel sound chip of a handheld console: one patch is one channel (Pulse, Wave or Noise) or a whole drum kit, with a stepped envelope and the chip tricks.

Hand-Type is our own design from general knowledge of such chips, not a copy of any chip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Channel picks what the patch is; only that channel's section matters.

  • Pulse: a pulse wave with four widths (Duty). A sweep can bend the pitch up or down in steps and, with Sweep Cut, end the note when it leaves the hearing range. Pulse 2 adds a second pulse, detuned, for a thicker lead.
  • Wave: a 32-step wave of 16 levels: eleven built-in tables, or User, drawn from 8 points. Levels 4 limits its volume to four steps, like the real chip's wave channel.
  • Noise: noise from a shift register, 15 or 7 bits long (Width). Shift and Divider set its rate, or Track makes it follow the note.
  • Drums: a kit by note, built from those channels: kick on C4 (60), blip 61, snare 62, clap 63 and 71, hats 64 (closed) to 67 (open), bell 68, crash 69, ride 70, and toms on 48 to 59. A hat cuts the hat before it. The Drums section shapes the kit.

The Envelope works in 16 steps: it starts at Init and moves one step every Step down to silence or up to full (Dir). Release Cut ends the note when it's released; Fade lets the envelope run down. Length can end a note after a set time.

Bits sets the output converter: 4 is the chip's own, 8 is clean. The Chip Tricks add the chip arpeggio, a stepped vibrato and a slide into each note.

The level of a second pulse played with the first.

  • 0 % is off.

docs.title: P2 Detune
docs.text:
The second pulse's tuning against the first, in cents.

  • 0 is unison; a few cents makes them beat.

docs.title: P2 Duty
docs.text:
The second pulse's width.

  • 12.5 %: a thin pulse.
  • 25 %: a narrow pulse.
  • 50 %: a square.
  • 75 %: the 25 % pulse upside down.

docs.title: Wave
docs.text: The wave channel: a 32-step wave from a table.

docs.title: Wave
docs.text:
Which table the wave channel plays.

  • Sine: a stepped sine.
  • Triangle: a stepped triangle.
  • Saw: a stepped saw.
  • Square 50: a square.
  • Square 25: a narrow pulse.
  • Organ: a built-in table.
  • Bass: a built-in table.
  • Buzz: a built-in table with sharp jumps.
  • Nasal: a built-in table.
  • Hollow: a built-in table.
  • Ramp 2: two saws per cycle: an octave up.
  • User: your own wave from User 1 to User 8.

docs.title: User 1
docs.text:
Point 1 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 2
docs.text:
Point 2 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 3
docs.text:
Point 3 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 4

Point 4 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 5

Point 5 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 6
docs.text:
Point 6 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 7
docs.text:
Point 7 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

  • 0 is the bottom of the wave; 15 the top.

docs.title: User 8

Point 8 of 8 of the User wave, 0 to 15.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
How many volume steps the wave channel has.

  • 4: four steps, like the real chip's wave channel.
  • 16: sixteen steps, as the other channels.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text: The noise channel: a shift register at a set rate or at the note.

docs.title: Width
docs.text:
The shift register's length.

  • 15 bit: a long sequence: plain noise.
  • 7 bit: a short loop of 127 steps: more tonal.

docs.title: Shift
docs.text:
Sets the noise rate: each step up halves it.

  • 0 is the highest; 13 the lowest.

docs.title: Divider
docs.text:
Divides the noise rate further.

  • 0 is the highest; 7 the lowest.

docs.title: Track
docs.text:
Whether the noise rate follows the note.

  • Off: Shift and Divider set the rate.
  • On: the rate follows the note played.

docs.title: Envelope
docs.text: The 16-step volume envelope, release and note length.

docs.title: Init
docs.text:
The level the envelope starts at.

  • 15 is full; 0 is silent.

docs.title: Dir
docs.text:
Which way the envelope moves while the note plays.

  • Down: falls to silence.
  • Up: rises to full.

docs.title: Step
docs.text:
How long each envelope step takes.

  • 16 ms: 16 ms per step: the fastest.
  • 31 ms: 31 ms per step.
  • 47 ms: 47 ms per step.
  • 62 ms: 62 ms per step.
  • 78 ms: 78 ms per step.
  • 94 ms: 94 ms per step.
  • 109 ms: 109 ms per step: the slowest.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
What happens when the note is released.

  • Cut: the note stops.
  • Fade: the envelope steps down to silence at Step.

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
Ends each note after a set time, held or not.

  • Off: notes last as long as they're held.
  • 62 ms: ends each note after 62 ms.
  • 125 ms: ends each note after 125 ms.
  • 188 ms: ends each note after 188 ms.
  • 250 ms: ends each note after 250 ms.
  • 312 ms: ends each note after 312 ms.
  • 375 ms: ends each note after 375 ms.
  • 438 ms: ends each note after 438 ms.

docs.title: Drums

docs.title: Kick Tune
docs.text:
The kick's pitch, in semitones.

docs.title: Kick Sweep
docs.text:
How fast the kick's pitch falls.

  • 1 is slow; 7 fast.

docs.title: Kick Decay
docs.text:
How long the kick rings.

  • 0 is shortest; 7 longest.

docs.title: Snare Width
docs.text:
The snare's noise.

docs.title: Snare Decay
docs.text:
How long the snare and the clap ring.

  • 0 is shortest; 7 longest.

docs.title: Hat Shift
docs.text:
The hats' noise rate.

docs.title: Hat Closed
docs.text:
How long the closed hat rings.

  • 0 is shortest; 7 longest.

docs.title: Hat Open
docs.text:
How long the open hat rings.

  • 0 is shortest; 7 longest.

docs.title: Crash Decay

How long the crash and ride ring.

docs.title: Blip Decay

docs.title: Chip Tricks
docs.text: The chip arpeggio, a stepped vibrato and a slide into each note.

docs.title: Arp Mode
docs.text:
Plays a fast chord from one note, the classic chip arpeggio.

  • Off: no arpeggio.
  • Oct: the note and the octave above.
  • Maj: a major chord: root, major 3rd, 5th.
  • Min: a minor chord: root, minor 3rd, 5th.
  • Sus4: root, 4th and 5th.
  • Dom7: a major chord with a minor 7th.
  • Maj7: a major chord with a major 7th.
  • Min7: a minor chord with a minor 7th.
  • Dim: root, minor 3rd, diminished 5th.
  • Aug: root, major 3rd, augmented 5th.
  • Pow5: root and 5th.
  • Custom: your own notes from Arp Note 2 and Arp Note 3.

docs.title: Arp Rate
docs.text:
How fast the arp steps through its notes.

  • 50 Hz: the European TV frame rate.
  • 60 Hz: the US and Japan TV frame rate.
  • 100 Hz: twice the European rate.
  • 120 Hz: twice the US and Japan rate.
  • 1/32: a step every 32nd note, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/48: 32nd-note triplets, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/64: a step every 64th note, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/96: 64th-note triplets, locked to the tempo.
  • 1/128: a step every 128th note, locked to the tempo.

docs.title: Arp Note 2
docs.text:
The second arp note, in semitones above the played one (Custom).

  • +3 minor 3rd, +4 major 3rd, +7 5th, +12 octave.

docs.title: Arp Note 3
docs.text:
The third arp note, in semitones above the played one (Custom).

  • +3 minor 3rd, +4 major 3rd, +7 5th, +12 octave.

docs.title: Vib Rate
docs.text:
How fast the vibrato goes up and down.

  • Low values are slow; high values fast.

docs.title: Vib Depth
docs.text:
How far the vibrato moves the pitch, in semitones.

  • 0 is off; higher values move the pitch further.

docs.title: Vib Delay
docs.text:
How long a note holds before the vibrato starts.

  • 0 starts the vibrato at once; longer values wait first.

docs.title: Slide Start
docs.text:
Starts this many semitones away and slides to the note.

  • Minus slides up into the note, plus slides down; 0 is off.

docs.title: Slide Time
docs.text:
How long that slide takes.

  • Short is a blip at the start; long is a swoop.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text: Glide, the output's bits, volume and stereo.

docs.title: Glide Mode
docs.text:
When one note slides into the next.

  • Always: every note slides from the last one.
  • Overlap: slides only when a note starts before the last one ends.
  • Legato: every note slides; overlapping notes don't restart the envelope.
  • Legato Overlap: only overlapping notes slide, and they don't restart the envelope.

docs.title: Glide Time
docs.text:
How long a glide takes.

  • 0 is no glide; longer values slide slowly between notes.

docs.title: Bits
docs.text:
How many bits the output has.

  • 4 is the chip's own; 8 is clean.

docs.title: Volume
docs.text:
The patch's own level.

  • 100 % is normal.

docs.title: Width
docs.text:
How wide the sound is in stereo.

  • 0 % is mono; 100 % is wide.

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
Spreads different notes left and right.

  • 0 % keeps every note in the middle.

docs.title: JU6
docs.text:
A polysynth with one oscillator per voice, a resonant filter, one envelope and a built-in stereo chorus, after the one-oscillator polysynths of the early 1980s.

JU6 is our own design from those instruments' owner's manuals, not a copy of any one of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each voice has one DCO. It plays a saw and a pulse, either one or both at once, plus a sub square one octave down and noise. The pulse's width is set by hand (PWM Manual) or swept by the LFO (PWM LFO).

The mix goes through a fixed high-pass (HPF: 0 boosts the bass, 1 is flat, 2 and 3 cut more and more low end) and then a 24 dB low-pass (VCF) with Resonance up to self-oscillation. The filter's cutoff moves with the envelope (Env, which can be negative), the LFO, the note played (Key Follow) and, through Velocity, how hard you play.

One ADSR envelope drives both the filter and the volume (VCA Env), or the volume just follows the note on and off (VCA Gate). One LFO (a triangle) is shared by all voices of the slot. LFO Delay holds it back at the start of each note and then fades it in. Vibrato sends it to the pitch, LFO in the VCF section sends it to the cutoff, and PWM LFO uses it for the pulse width.

The chorus works on all the voices together and makes the sound stereo. I and II are two fixed speeds and depths; I+II runs both at once.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: What each setting does, as the Edit Patch help box shows it.

docs.title: Oscillator
docs.text: The voice's one oscillator: saw, pulse, sub and noise, mixed.

docs.title: Saw
docs.text:
Whether the saw wave plays.

  • Off: no saw.
  • On: the saw plays, alone or with the pulse.

docs.title: Pulse
docs.text:
Whether the pulse wave plays.

  • Off: no pulse.
  • On: the pulse plays, alone or with the saw.

docs.title: PW
docs.text:
The pulse width by hand, or how far the LFO sweeps it (PWM LFO).

  • 0 % is a square; 100 % is a thin 5 % pulse.

docs.title: PWM
docs.text:
What sets the pulse width.

  • Manual: PW sets the width and it stays put.
  • LFO: the LFO sweeps the width; PW sets how far.

docs.title: Sub
docs.text:
A square wave one octave below the note.

  • 0 % is off; turn it up for more low end.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
White noise mixed into the oscillator.

  • 0 % is off; turn it up for breath or hiss.

docs.title: Vibrato
docs.text:
How much the LFO moves the pitch.

  • 0 % is off; 100 % is 2 semitones either way.

docs.title: HPF / VCF
docs.text: The filters: a fixed high-pass, then a resonant low-pass.

docs.title: HPF
docs.text:
The fixed high-pass before the low-pass.

  • 0 Boost: lifts the bass a little.
  • 1 Flat: no high-pass.
  • 2: cuts the low end below about 240 Hz.
  • 3: cuts more low end, below about 720 Hz.

docs.title: Cutoff
docs.text:
Where the low-pass filter starts to cut.

  • Low is dark and muffled; high lets everything through.

docs.title: Resonance
docs.text:
How much the filter rings at the cutoff.

  • 0 % is smooth; near 100 % the filter whistles on its own.

docs.title: Env
docs.text:
How much the envelope moves the cutoff; minus moves it down.

  • 100 % sweeps up to 7 octaves; 0 % leaves the cutoff still.

docs.title: LFO
docs.text:
How much the LFO moves the cutoff.

  • 0 % is off; 100 % moves it 3 octaves either way.

docs.title: Key Follow
docs.text:
How much the cutoff follows the note played.

  • 100 % moves the cutoff an octave per octave; 0 % keeps it fixed.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text:
How much playing harder opens the envelope's cutoff sweep.

  • 0 % ignores velocity; 100 % makes soft notes sweep little.

docs.title: Amplifier
docs.text: How the volume follows the note, and the patch level.

docs.title: VCA
docs.text:
What shapes the volume of each note.

  • Env: the ADSR envelope shapes the volume.
  • Gate: full volume while the note is held, silent after it.

docs.title: Volume
docs.text:
The patch's own level.

  • 100 % is normal.

docs.title: Width
docs.text:
How wide the sound is in stereo.

  • 0 % is mono; 100 % is wide.

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
Spreads different notes left and right.

  • 0 % keeps every note in the middle.

docs.title: Envelope
docs.text: One ADSR for the filter (Env) and the volume (VCA Env).

docs.title: Attack
docs.text:
How long a note takes to reach full level.

  • 0 starts at once; higher values fade in.

docs.title: Decay
docs.text:
How long the note takes to fall from full level to Sustain.

  • Short is plucky; long rings out.

docs.title: Sustain
docs.text:
The level held while the note is down.

  • 0 % dies away after Decay; 100 % stays at full level.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
How long the note fades after it ends.

  • 0 stops at once; higher values leave a tail.

docs.title: LFO
docs.text: The slow triangle wave shared by all the slot's voices.

docs.title: LFO Rate
docs.text:
How fast the LFO moves.

  • Low values sweep slowly; high values wobble fast.

docs.title: LFO Delay
docs.text:
How long each note waits before the LFO fades in.

  • 0 starts the LFO at once; longer waits, then fades it in.

docs.title: Chorus
docs.text: The built-in stereo chorus on all voices together.

docs.title: Chorus
docs.text:
Which chorus mode plays.

  • Off: no chorus; the sound stays mono.
  • I: the slower, gentler chorus.
  • II: the faster, deeper chorus.
  • I+II: both at once.

docs.title: PERC
docs.text:
A drum machine after the Tracker Mini's PERC: one patch is a kit of six drums, each with its own mixer channel, and a waveshaper and EQ on the kit.

PERC's sound engine is our own design, built to the Tracker Mini's PERC settings.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each note plays one drum:

Note Drum 60 (C4) kick 62 snare 64 to 67 hi-hat, closed to open 69 cymbal 71 percussion 61, 63, 68, 70 nothing every other note the tom, at that note's pitch

A note restarts its own drum and leaves the others ringing; the hats are one channel, so a closed hat cuts an open one. Up to five drums ring at once.

The kick, tom and snare have a Body Wave: one of 16 families, each starting at a sine (0 %) and morphing into its own shape as the percentage goes up:

  • Sat-Sin, Triangle, Square: towards a soft-clipped sine, a triangle, a square.
  • Square FM, FM1, FM3, FM7, FM11: the sine's phase pushed by a square, or by a sine at 1, 3, 7 or 11 times its pitch.
  • tzFM1 to tzFM11: a harder FM at those ratios, with some AM.
  • Glitch 1 to Glitch 4: the sine's phase in fewer steps, its level in fewer steps, folded, or its phase scrambled.

The hi-hat and the cymbal mix a metal tone with noise: six squares (Classic) or two-operator FM (FM), shaped by Timbre.

The Mixer gives each drum a level, pan, Delay and Reverb send and an Output: through the waveshaper and EQ (Main), the EQ only (Post Overdrive), or neither (Post EQ). The FX are a waveshaper and a 3-band EQ on the kit.

There's no Volume setting: use the slot's Gain.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: What each setting does, as the Edit Patch help box shows it.

docs.title: Kick
docs.text: The kick (note 60): a body wave with a transient and a modulation envelope.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
How the kick's oscillator and modulation work.

  • Classic8: the oscillator runs free; Mod moves the wave.
  • Synced8: the oscillator restarts at each hit; Mod moves the wave.
  • Classic9: restarts at each hit; Mod moves the pitch, 4 octaves at 100.

docs.title: Pitch
docs.text:
The kick's pitch, as a note.

  • Low notes are lower; high notes higher.

docs.title: Body Attack
docs.text:
How long the body takes to rise, in ms.

  • 0 starts at once.

docs.title: Body Decay
docs.text:
How long the body rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Mod Decay
docs.text:
How long the modulation envelope takes to fall.

  • Short is a quick blip; long a slow sweep.

docs.title: Mod Amount
docs.text:
How much the modulation moves the wave or the pitch (Model); minus reverses it.

  • 0 is off.

docs.title: Body Wave
docs.text:
The kick's waveform: one of 16 families, and how far it morphs from a sine.

  • At 0 % every family is a sine; 100 % is the family's own shape.

docs.title: Trans Timbre
docs.text:
The transient at the start: plus a click, minus a noise burst; further out is brighter.

  • 0 is the darkest; 100 a bright click, -100 a bright noise burst.

docs.title: Trans Level
docs.text:
The level of the transient.

  • 0 % is no transient.

docs.title: Toms
docs.text: The tom: every note not used by another drum, at that note's pitch.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
How the tom is built.

  • Classic: one body wave.
  • Classic+: one body wave plus a noise attack.
  • Resonant: three detuned oscillators plus a noise attack.

docs.title: Body Wave
docs.text:
The tom's waveform: one of 16 families, and how far it morphs from a sine.

  • At 0 % every family is a sine; 100 % is the family's own shape.

docs.title: Body Attack
docs.text:
How long the body takes to rise, in ms.

  • 0 starts at once.

docs.title: Body Decay
docs.text:
How long the tom rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Mod Decay
docs.text:
How long the modulation envelope takes to fall.

  • Short is a quick blip; long a slow sweep.

docs.title: Pitch Mod
docs.text:
How far the modulation moves the pitch: 3 semitones per 100; minus is down.

  • 0 is off.

docs.title: Wave Mod
docs.text:
How much the modulation moves the wave; minus reverses it.

  • 0 is off.

docs.title: Trans Timbre
docs.text:
The noise attack's filter (Classic+ and Resonant), from 100 Hz to 10 kHz.

  • 0 is the darkest; 200 the brightest.

docs.title: Trans Level
docs.text:
The level of the noise attack (Classic+ and Resonant).

  • 0 % is no noise attack.

docs.title: Snare
docs.text: The snare (note 62): a body wave and a sine partner, plus a noise snap.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
How the snare is built: the partner's tuning, the sweep and the noise filter.

  • Classic8: high-passed noise, no sweep.
  • Classic9: band-passed noise and a pitch sweep.
  • Classic9+: brighter, with a deeper sweep.
  • Modern: a resonant band-pass on the noise, no sweep.
  • Modern+: a small sweep and a saturated body.

docs.title: Pitch
docs.text:
The snare body's pitch, as a note.

  • Low notes are lower; high notes higher.

docs.title: Tone
docs.text:
The balance between the body wave and its sine partner.

  • 0 % and 100 % are the two ends.

docs.title: Body Wave
docs.text:
The snare's waveform: one of 16 families, and how far it morphs from a sine.

  • At 0 % every family is a sine; 100 % is the family's own shape.

docs.title: Body Decay
docs.text:
How long the body rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Snap Attack
docs.text:
How long the noise snap takes to rise, in ms.

  • 0 starts at once.

docs.title: Snap Decay
docs.text:
How long the noise snap rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Snap Timbre
docs.text:
Where the snap's filter sits, from 800 Hz to 12.8 kHz.

  • Low is darker; high is brighter.

docs.title: Body/Snap Mix
docs.text:
The balance of body and snap.

  • 0 is both; minus is more body, plus more snap.

docs.title: Hi Hat
docs.text: The hi-hat (notes 64 to 67, closed to open): metal and noise, filtered.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
How the metal tone is made.

  • Classic: six squares around Tone Pitch.
  • FM: two-operator FM; Timbre picks one of 25 settings.

docs.title: Timbre
docs.text:
Classic: how far apart the six squares are; FM: which of 25 settings.

  • Classic 0 is all at Tone Pitch; 12 the classic spread, 24 twice that.

docs.title: Closed Decay
docs.text:
How long the closed hat rings (note 64).

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Open Decay
docs.text:
How long the open hat rings (note 67); 65 and 66 sit between.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Decay Shape
docs.text:
The shape of the hat's fade.

  • 0 % is a natural, curved fade; 100 % a straight line.

docs.title: HPF Cutoff
docs.text:
Where the high-pass cuts the lows.

  • Low keeps more body; high is thinner.

docs.title: LPF Cutoff
docs.text:
Where the low-pass cuts the highs.

  • Low is darker; high is brighter.

docs.title: Tone Pitch
docs.text:
The pitch of the metal tone.

  • Low values are darker; high values brighter.

docs.title: Tone/Noise Mix
docs.text:
The balance of metal tone and noise.

  • 0 is both; minus is more tone, plus more noise.

docs.title: Cymbal
docs.text: The cymbal (note 69): metal and noise through a body and an impact stage.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
How the metal tone is made.

  • Classic: six squares around Tone Pitch.
  • FM: two-operator FM; Timbre picks one of 25 settings.

docs.title: Timbre
docs.text:
Classic: how far apart the six squares are; FM: which of 25 settings.

  • Classic 0 is all at Tone Pitch; 12 the classic spread, 24 twice that.

docs.title: Body Filter
docs.text:
Where the body's band-pass sits.

  • Low is darker; high is brighter.

docs.title: Impact Filter
docs.text:
Where the impact's high-pass sits.

  • Low is fuller; high is thinner.

docs.title: Body Decay
docs.text:
How long the body rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Impact Decay
docs.text:
How long the impact rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Tone Pitch
docs.text:
The pitch of the metal tone.

  • Low values are darker; high values brighter.

docs.title: Tone/Noise Mix
docs.text:
The balance of metal tone and noise.

  • 0 is both; minus is more tone, plus more noise.

docs.title: Impact/Body Mix
docs.text:
The balance of the impact and body stages.

  • 0 is both; minus is more impact, plus more body.

docs.title: Percussion
docs.text: The percussion (note 71): one of five models.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Which percussion sound plays.

  • Clap: bursts of band-passed noise and a tail.
  • Clap+: a second clap model.
  • Maracas: high-passed noise.
  • Shaker: band-passed noise with a swell.
  • Cowbell: two squares through a band-pass.

docs.title: Variation
docs.text:
Clap: the burst spacing; Maracas: random decay; Shaker: the swell; Cowbell: the interval.

  • 0 is the least; 100 the most.

docs.title: Timbre
docs.text:
The filter or the pitch of the percussion.

  • Low is darker or lower; high brighter or higher.

docs.title: Decay
docs.text:
How long the tail rings.

  • Short stops quickly; long rings on.

docs.title: Mixer
docs.text: Each drum's level, pan, sends and where it goes.

docs.title: Kick Level
docs.text:
The kick's level.

  • 100 % is normal; 0 % is silent.

docs.title: Kick Pan
docs.text:
Where the kick sits left to right.

  • 0 is the middle.

docs.title: Kick Delay
docs.text:
How much of the kick goes to the Delay.

  • 0 sends none.

docs.title: Kick Reverb
docs.text:
How much of the kick goes to the Reverb.

  • 0 sends none.

docs.title: Kick Output
docs.text:
Where the kick goes: through the FX or past them.

  • Main: through the waveshaper and the EQ.
  • Post Overdrive: past the waveshaper, through the EQ.
  • Post EQ: past both.

docs.title: Tom Level
docs.text:
The tom's level.

  • 100 % is normal; 0 % is silent.

docs.title: Tom Pan
docs.text:
Where the tom sits left to right.

  • 0 is the middle.

docs.title: Tom Delay
docs.text:
How much of the tom goes to the Delay.

  • 0 sends none.

docs.title: Tom Reverb
docs.text:
How much of the tom goes to the Reverb.

  • 0 sends none.

docs.title: Tom Output
docs.text:
Where the tom goes: through the FX or past them.

  • Main: through the waveshaper and the EQ.
  • Post Overdrive: past the waveshaper, through the EQ.
  • Post EQ: past both.

docs.title: Snare Level
docs.text:
The snare's level.

  • 100 % is normal; 0 % is silent.

docs.title: T-Type
docs.text:
A drum synth after the classic transistor drum machines: one patch is a kit of ten drum channels, every drum built from sines with pitch sweeps, filtered noise, struck resonators and a bank of six square oscillators.

T-Type is our own design from those machines' owner's manuals, not a copy of any of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each note plays one drum:

Note Drum 60 (C4) kick 61 rim 62 snare 63, 71 clap 64 to 67 hi-hat, closed to open 68 cowbell 69 crash 70 ride 48 to 51, 52 to 55, 56 to 59 low, mid and high tom, a semitone up per note

Notes from 72 up repeat 60 to 71; notes below 48 play the low tom lower. These match PERC's kick, snare and hats.

The hats are one channel, so a closed hat cuts an open one; the crash and the ride share the cymbal channel. Up to eight drums ring at once.

Every drum has a Character: three variants of how it's built. Each drum also has its own Delay and Reverb send (Sends section), and a fixed place in the stereo field that Width spreads.

Accent sets how much velocity changes each hit's level. Drive saturates the whole kit. There's no Volume setting: use the slot's Gain.
